newsitem.title: USA: U.S. report finds power lines pose no health risk.
newsitem.headline: U.S. report finds power lines pose no health risk.

text.p: In 17 years of research, scientists have found no hard proof that electric power lines near homes are a health hazard, the National Research Council said on Thursday.

"Specifically, no conclusive and consistent evidence shows that exposures to residential electric and magnetic fields produce cancer, adverse neurobehavioral effects or reproductive and developmental effects," the council said in a report reviewing 500 previous studies.

The studies focused on health effects of magnetic fields -- considered the main potential threat -- created by power lines, wires and electric appliances such as hair dryers, microwave ovens, and computer terminals. Appliances create the highest field strengths to which people are commonly exposed.
Concern about electromagnetic fields grew after research in 1979 found that children living near power lines had higher rates of leukaemia than other children.

But the council said childhood leukaemia research to date was flawed because it measured exposure by estimating magnetic fields inside homes based on the distance of the power lines from the homes, current and size of the wires. It said actual measurements of magnetic field strengths inside homes showed little correlation to ratings of the wires outside the home.
"No evidence links contemporary measurements of magnetic-field levels to childhood leukaemia," the report said.

"All we can do is say living near power lines has a statistical association with childhood leukaemia, but we don't know what the cause is," said Dr. Charles Stevens, a professor at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Salk Institute in California who led the 16-member panel reviewing the studies.
Calling for more research, the council said the leukaemia tie might instead be due to other factors, such as the age of homes, pollution and heavy traffic in areas near power lines.

Laboratory tests exposing animals to the low-frequency magnetic fields common in homes did not cause cancer, even at high doses, and did not harm animal reproduction, development or behaviour, the report said.
Similarly, tests on tissues and cells found no damage from low-frequency magnetic fields. If anything, magnetic fields might have had some benefit, aiding bone healing in animals.

"Science can never really prove that anything is safe," David Savitz, a professor of epidemiology at the University of North Carolina, told a new conference. With this report, he said, scientists have simply "failed to find a hazard."

But the National Research Council called for more research into the link between high exposure to electromagnetic fields and breast cancer in animals already exposed to other cancer-causing agents. More research is also needed on why electromagnetic fields appear to affect the levels of the hormone melatonin in animals but not in people, it said.
The report did not discuss concerns about electromagnetic fields created by cellular telephones.
The three-year review was called for by Congress and sponsored by the Energy Department.

While utilities felt vindicated by the report, they said they hoped it would not discourage Congress from continuing funding of a five-year joint government and industry research programme on electromagnetic fields that began in 1994.
"We've felt all along that there weren't enough lab studies," said Mary Kenkel, a spokeswoman for the Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities.
